correctness.rationale: The exact finite birth–death transition ratio yields strictly positive stationary weights. All hypotheses ensure 0<d<=m<a1<a2, so the logarithms are finite and positive. The ratio of the two positive integral kernels is strictly increasing in integration variable and therefore its weighted average F(d) strictly increases in d. This forces at most one sign change in inward relative likelihood, with exact sharp endpoint cutoffs. Reflection makes the same comparison valid for the radial masses; standard single-crossing sums prove strict tails; symmetric convex averages prove the convex-order consequences. Integer cross-product checker confirms 38,556 detailed balance and 87,808 likelihood-ratio sign comparisons, plus the exact three-regime example. Finite tests do not replace any quantified analytical step.

originality.rationale: The exact reversible stationary formula and qualitative bimodality are explicitly credited to Mobilia (2015). The full finite-S two-control likelihood-ratio classification, its two sharp distinct thresholds and the intermediate one-turn regime require a monotone ratio of logarithmic kernel integrals; these are not stated in the examined 2015 text or the heterogeneous 2016 text. Nearby studies of anchored voter dynamics on cycles or deterministic opinion models do not cover this comparison; no equivalent theorem was identified in the inspected literature. Priority remains provisional because a general total-positivity theorem might subsume the result.

value.rationale: The comparison answers a substantive control-interaction question in a classic finite social-influence model: whether increasing the unanimity consultation requirement can offset an increase in equal numbers of committed agents, uniformly across all polarization tails. Sharp distinct cutoffs determine two regions with strict distribution-wide and convex order, while the intermediate one-turn relative likelihood reveals a transition invisible to single-parameter qualitative phase descriptions. Keeping susceptible count fixed avoids a normalization artifact. The result is an idealized analytic benchmark, not an empirical intervention claim.
